conversation.content:
[Soft smile] Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a well-tested questionnaire that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally during the first weeks and months after birth.  

Everything we talk about will stay just between you and our care team; we want you to feel completely safe and not judged. The EPDS has 10 questions about your mood, worries, and how you’ve been coping over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—we just want to hear what’s true for you. When you’re ready, we’ll go through each question together.  

Before we start, do you have any questions for me? …Okay, let’s begin.  

**Question 1:** Over the last seven days, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has it felt hard to find pleasure in anything?

[She shifts in the chair, rocking the stroller gently with one foot.]

Honestly? Things just feel… flatter. Like, I still enjoy my coffee and a quick show on my phone when the baby naps, but it’s not the same spark. Even holding him—of course I love him—but sometimes I’m too tired to feel that big rush everyone talks about.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[Small shrug, eyes on the baby for a second.]

I do laugh—maybe a couple of times—but it feels like I have to work for it. My husband will crack a joke and I’ll chuckle, yet it fades fast. Nothing feels light like it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[She rubs her thumb along the stroller handle, voice quiet.]

Not really. I mean, I still plan stuff—like taking him for his two-month pictures tomorrow—but it’s more something I “should” do than something I’m excited about. The happy anticipation just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[She gives a soft, rueful laugh.]

More times than I’d like to admit. Yesterday he spit up a ton after I fed him and I kept thinking, “Did I eat something that upset his stomach?” Or if he won’t nap, I immediately assume I’m doing the routine wrong. Rationally I know babies just spit up and fight sleep, but the voice in my head still says, “You should’ve figured it out by now.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[She tucks a loose strand of hair behind her ear, bouncing her knee nervously.]

Yeah… like, I’ll be staring at the baby monitor convinced he’s breathing too fast, even though the pediatrician said everything looks fine. Or I lie awake imagining I’ll trip on the stairs while holding him. Nothing’s actually happened, but the worry just keeps looping.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[She hugs her arms across her chest, voice a little shaky.]

A couple of times—especially at night—this wave of fear hits out of nowhere. My heart races and I feel like I can’t get a full breath. I know nothing’s wrong, but for a minute it’s like my body thinks something awful is about to happen.
Things have been getting on top of me

[She exhales slowly, shoulders sagging.]

Most days, yeah. It’s not that any single thing is impossible, it’s just the constant loop—feed, burp, change, try to nap, dishes, laundry, pump, start over. By late afternoon I feel like I’m drowning in small tasks and I can’t see the end of it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[She glances down at her hands, voice low.]

I wouldn’t say “unhappy” exactly keeps me awake—more like my mind won’t shut off. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed, and suddenly I’m replaying every little thing I did that day, worrying I’ll oversleep and miss a feeding. Some nights I’m still wide-eyed at two a.m., even though I’m dead tired.
I have felt sad or miserable

[She nods slowly, eyes a bit glassy.]

Yeah… not every minute, but it hits, especially when the house is quiet. I’ll be folding onesies and this heavy sadness just settles in—like I’m grieving something, only I can’t name what it is.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[She gives a small shake of her head, swallowing hard.]

Not really. I’ve teared up once or twice—like when the lactation consultant mentioned low weight gain—but full crying? No. Mostly the sadness just sits in my chest without spilling over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[She looks up quickly, eyes widening.]

No—never. I could never do that to my baby or my family. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I want to be here for him. I just need help feeling like myself again.

You've shared that the last couple of months have felt heavy and flat; even when you manage a laugh or plan an outing, the spark quickly fades. You're working tirelessly to care for your baby, yet you often feel overwhelmed by the endless routine and are haunted by worries that something might go wrong. Sadness settles in unexpectedly, and nighttime brings a racing mind and brief waves of panic, even though you're exhausted. Despite all this, you remain committed to your baby and family, and you've never thought of harming yourself-you simply want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports limited, effortful laughter that quickly fades and lacks previous lightness, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "the happy anticipation just isn't there," matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('more times than I'd like to admit') with multiple recent examples, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, intrusive, unfounded worries occurring nightly, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden waves of fear with physical panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness) occurring multiple times, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage the relentless cycle of tasks and feeling like "drowning," aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent nighttime rumination and difficulty falling asleep despite exhaustion, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, noticeable sadness that "settles in" during quiet moments, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 21 places you well above the cutoff (≥14) indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Key items align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, significant anxiety, sleep disturbance not solely due to infant care, and impaired daily functioning. <quote>The happy anticipation just isn't there</quote> and <quote>I feel like I'm drowning</quote> typify the mood and functional impact reported. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to discuss these results and consider therapy or medication options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health therapist</med> or psychiatrist experienced in <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>anxiety</med>
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2-4 weeks to monitor progress
4. Reach out today to a support group for new moms or <med>postpartum support international</med> warm-line for encouragement
5. Practice brief relaxation techniques (paced breathing, progressive muscle relaxation) when panic sensations arise
6. Share these findings with a trusted partner, friend, or family member so they can help with baby care and household tasks
7. Discuss safe, short-term sleep strategies-possibly splitting night duties with a partner-to gain longer continuous rest
8. Keep a simple symptom diary noting mood, anxiety spikes, and sleep hours to review with your clinician
9. Seek immediate help from your provider or local emergency services if you ever develop thoughts of self-harm or feel unsafe
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: 2-month postpartum mother, first-person report via structured interview (date/time not specified)

Screening tool: Edinburgh-like 10-item query

Key endorsed items  
- Anhedonia: marked reduction in spontaneous pleasure/laughter; anticipatory enjoyment absent  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care (“should have figured it out”)  
- Persistent, intrusive anxiety (baby’s breathing, falling, “looping” worries)  
- Panic-type episodes (sudden racing heart, breathlessness, no clear trigger)  
- Sense of being overwhelmed by routine tasks; “drowning” by afternoon  
- Sleep disturbance unrelated to infant demands (racing mind, early insomnia)  
- Sad/miserable mood with unnamed grief; tearfulness short of full crying spells  
- Denies any self-harm ideation; protective of infant and family

Pattern summary  
Consistent cluster of low mood, loss of enjoyment, heightened anxiety/rumination, and functional difficulty coping—meets screening threshold for probable **postpartum depression with prominent anxiety**.  
No acute safety concerns reported; no suicidal or infanticidal thoughts elicited.

Screening significance  
High likelihood of major depressive episode, peripartum-onset, with comorbid anxiety features; warrants formal diagnostic evaluation and discussion of support / treatment options.
